The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2022-02-10.145.2) "*that clause (c)(i) be agreed to.*" ### What is clause (c)(i)? > *(c) the routine of business from 4.30 pm, or after consideration of the [Mitochondrial Donation Law Reform (Maeve's Law) Bill 2021](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6697) concludes, whichever is earlier, be consideration of the following items:* > >> *(i) [Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6784)*

The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2022-02-10.177.1) introduced by Tasmanian Senator [Nick McKim](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/tasmania/nick_mckim) (Greens), which means they failed. Senator McKim [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2022-02-10.172.3): > *This amendment would prevent listed companies from holding wholly virtual AGMs. It's been revised to align it with the amendments agreed to in the House to establish a review into these provisions of the bill. By their nature, listed companies have a public responsibility and the parliament should ensure that their AGMs are conducted in a publicly observable manner. Allowing listed companies to hold hybrid AGMs will provide an opportunity for all of the issues associated with virtual meetings to be sorted out and for there to be a real-world confirmation of their purported benefits. Until then, wholly virtual AGMs for listed companies should not be allowed and shareholders should retain the opportunity to sit in the same room as the executive and the board to bear witness to exactly what they are up to and have the capacity to hold them to account for their actions.* ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd037), the bill was introduced in order to: > * *allow companies to use technology to execute company documents such as contracts and deeds and to also sign meetings-related documents and provide those to their members and* > * *allow companies and registered schemes to hold hybrid meetings (which give members the option of either attending in person or remotely).*

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2022-02-10.181.1) to pass the bill in the Senate. In parliamentary jargon, they voted to read the bill [for a third time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). Because the bill has already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. ### What does the bill do? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd037), the bill was introduced in order to: > * *allow companies to use technology to execute company documents such as contracts and deeds and to also sign meetings-related documents and provide those to their members and* > * *allow companies and registered schemes to hold hybrid meetings (which give members the option of either attending in person or remotely).*

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 permanently allows companies, registered schemes and their officers to use digital technologies for meetings, sending materials and executing documents, replacing temporary COVID-19 relief expiring 31 March 2022. It requires companies to give shareholders a reasonable opportunity to participate, including speaking or asking questions orally and in writing, and allows shareholders with at least 5% voting power to request an independent report on a poll.

The speaker supported making virtual annual general meetings permanent but moved an amendment for an independent review within two years, focusing on whether small shareholders can still hold directors to account.

The speaker supported the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, arguing its two core elements—expanding electronic document signing and allowing virtual or hybrid annual general meetings—will increase efficiency, transparency, and shareholder access, particularly for smaller investors who previously could not attend physical meetings.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, which enables virtual and hybrid AGMs, should balance accessibility benefits against the reduced scrutiny and engagement of shareholders, noting the Australian Shareholders Association's criticism that virtual meetings lack dynamism and accountability compared to in-person formats. The speech also paid tribute to historian Stuart Macintyre, citing his works like *The History Wars* and *Australia's Boldest Experiment*.

The speaker argued that the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 should make permanent the temporary relief allowing companies to hold meetings electronically and execute documents digitally, citing positive pandemic experiences and increased shareholder participation.

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 would increase flexibility for listed companies and shareholder-board interactions, with Labor’s opposition unsurprising given their history.

The speaker argued in support of the Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021, which makes permanent temporary COVID-19 relief allowing companies to hold hybrid meetings and use electronic signatures, reducing regulatory burden and saving an estimated $430 million per year for 10 years.

The Corporations Amendment (Meetings and Documents) Bill 2021 permanently allows companies to hold physical, hybrid, or virtual meetings (if permitted by their constitution), receive documents electronically or in hard copy, and execute documents using electronic or wet-ink signatures, with a 12-month opt-in review of annual general meetings.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?id=2021-10-21.147.2) to agree with the main idea of the following two bills: * the [Customs Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6756); and * the [Customs Tariff Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r6757). In parliamentary jargon, the majority voted to read these bills for a [second time](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/bills-and-laws/making-a-law-in-the-australian-parliament/). ### What is the main idea of these bills? According to the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd2122a/22bd024): > *The purpose of the two Bills is to amend the Customs Act 1901 and the Customs Tariff Act 1995 to implement Australia’s commitments under the [Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_Comprehensive_Economic_Partnership).* > > *Two separate Bills are needed in order to comply with the Australian constitutional requirement that ‘laws imposing duties of customs shall deal with duties of customs only’ and provisions regarding other matters must be dealt with separately. As such, the Customs Act sets out the broad administrative rules regarding the export and import of goods, while the Customs Tariff Act focuses exclusively on the tariff/customs duty rates applicable to imported goods.*

The bill implements the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (RCEP), the world's largest free trade agreement covering 15 signatories including Australia, ASEAN, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea, which accounts for nearly 60% of Australia's trade and two-thirds of exports. The bill inserts rules of origin and document retention requirements into the Customs Act 1901.

The Customs Tariff Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021 implements Australia's import tariff commitments under the RCEP by inserting a new schedule of duty rates, eliminating duties for most originating goods over time, and retaining customs duty on excise equivalent goods such as fuel, alcohol, tobacco and petroleum products.

Labor supported the RCEP implementation bills while moving a second reading amendment calling for transparency in trade negotiations, no labour market testing waivers, and targeted sanctions against Myanmar's military regime, and confirmed that the agreement does not undermine Australian workers, public services, or domestic laws.

The speaker argued in favour of the Customs Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021, highlighting the benefits of free trade for Australia’s economy, jobs, and regional security. They noted the RCEP includes 15 nations (ASEAN, New Zealand, South Korea, Japan, China, and Australia), expressed disappointment that India is not part of the agreement, and referenced past work at the wool company Michell to illustrate the importance of export markets in Asia.

The speaker argued that the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) offers limited new market access, providing only 94% of existing tariff-free coverage even when fully matured, and lacks commitments on environmental protection, workers' rights, and human rights. They noted that Australia has five separate trade agreements with Malaysia, that no independent economic analysis of the RCEP was provided, and that a reservation was lodged for child care but not aged care, raising concerns about future regulation.

The speaker supported the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the RCEP agreement, arguing it builds confidence for Australian exporters in Asia, particularly small- to medium-sized businesses. They noted the agreement adds little for large firms already in bilateral deals but creates new opportunities for SMEs, citing local exporters like Frosty Boy, Teys abattoirs, and BlockTexx, and named 15 participating countries including Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, China, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea.

The speaker argued that the RCEP agreement will lower tariffs and provide favourable arrangements for Australian exporters, particularly in agriculture and food processing. They highlighted the importance of a rules-based trade order to protect exporters, noted the loss of manufacturing industries like motor vehicles and wool processing, and expressed hope for future trade deals, including with the European Union.

The Customs Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021 was argued to ratify the world's largest free trade agreement, covering 29% of global GDP and 15 countries including China, with benefits for Australian services exports and a single set of rules for exporters, while containing no investor-state dispute settlement clauses. The speaker also condemned human rights abuses in Myanmar and suggested Myanmar could be admitted then suspended from the agreement.

The speaker argued in support of the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills to implement the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (RCEP), a free trade agreement with 14 Indo-Pacific nations covering 30% of global GDP and population. He noted the agreement's benefits for his electorate of Barker, particularly for food manufacturing and digital services, and paid tribute to former MP Bert Kelly for his historic advocacy of free trade.

The speaker strongly supported the Customs Amendment (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement Implementation) Bill 2021, arguing it would reduce compliance burdens for Australian importers and exporters through simpler rules of origin and improve access to 15 markets including China, Japan, and South Korea. They highlighted that Australia’s trade surplus reached $15 billion in August 2021, attributed free trade agreements to higher agricultural prices (e.g., canola near $1,000/tonne, lamb at $8/kg), and called for further trade deals with India, the EU, and the Gulf states.

Argued that committing to net zero emissions by 2050 while China, a partner in the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, faces no such constraint puts Australia at a disadvantage, a position he said over 95 per cent of politicians in this parliament support, and called for Magnitsky-style sanctions over Myanmar's human rights abuses while saying Australia should address its own police violence against protesters and pandemic restrictions first.

The speaker argued that the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills, implementing the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) with 14 Indo-Pacific nations, will boost trade, lower prices for consumers, and aid pandemic recovery with no cost to customs duty receipts. The speaker also thanked the trade minister for a $1.2 billion tourism package and half-price airfares, and criticised the Queensland Premier for border closures costing Gold Coast tourism $1 billion.

The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, signed by Australia and 14 other countries in November 2020, required amendments to the Customs Act and Customs Tariff Act to implement preferential trade rules and create new opportunities for Australian exporters across the Indo-Pacific.

Labor opposed the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Political Campaigners) Bill 2021, arguing it would lower the political campaigner threshold for charities and not-for-profits from $500,000 or two-thirds of annual income to $100,000 or one-third, imposing heavy disclosure requirements and foreign-donation bans that silence critics.
